newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba annoyed by cancellation of Spain credit line.
newsitem.headline: Cuba annoyed by cancellation of Spain credit line.

text.p: Cuban Trade Minister Ricardo Cabrisas on Thursday expressed irritation with Spain over the cancellation of a $15 million credit line for exports of Spanish industrial goods that Cuba was aiming to use in its sugar sector.
Spain canceled the credit line last month, citing technical reasons. It was approved in late 1995.
Cabrisas, in an interview with the Cuban news agency Prensa Latina, said Cuba considered the decision "incomprehensible" and added, "There must be other reasons for the cancellation".

Cabrisas suggested the move could be political, noting that the conservative government of Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar has taken a more hard-line stance on Cuba since it took over from the Socialists last May.

Tension between the two countries boiled over last November when Havana retracted official approval for a new Spanish ambassador, saying Madrid was interfering in its internal affairs with constant criticism of the Cuban political system. However, both sides have since sought to ease tensions.

Cabrisas said Cuba had complained to the Spanish Trade Ministry about the credit cancellation, saying it was concerned the decision did not correspond to a trend of increased bilateral trade. Spain had not yet replied, he added.
The Spanish Foreign Ministry earlier this week said there was no political aim behind the cancellation of the credit line, but that it had not been used for more than a year.
Spokesman Inocencio Arias told Spanish media that three other lines of credit with Cuba, with ceilings of $80 million, $60 million and $40 million, remained open.

Cabrisas said the cancellation of the credit meant it was now necessary to look for other ways to finance supplies for the sugar sector. He added that for technical reasons, it would not be possible to transfer previously negotiated contracts to one of the other three credit lines.
After the agreement for the credit in November 1995 at a meeting of the joint Cuba-Spain economic commission, Cuba prepared contracts with various Spanish suppliers, Cabrisas said.

Havana presented the necessary documentation to the Spanish credit insurance group Compania Espanola de Seguro de Credito a la Exportacion, or CESCE, last October, when the accord was still valid, Cabrisas said.
In January, Spanish authorities informed Cuba the credit operations had not been approved for technical reasons, the Cuban minister said.
According to Cabrisas, bilateral trade between Spain and Cuba last year was worth about $562 million, making it one of Cuba's leading trade partners.
